It avoids scrotal violation, reduces tumour seeding and allows proper lymphatic staging.

faq.a: Acute bacterial prostatitis is common, but chronic prostatitis may be inflammatory or sterile; urine culture guides therapy.

exam: A 22‑year‑old presents with 4 h of sudden left testicular pain and absent cremasteric reflex — what is the next step and why? — Immediate surgical exploration; time‑critical to salvage the testis.

A 35‑year‑old with HIV has a painless penile ulcer and indurated base — which test confirms the diagnosis and what is the treatment? — Rapid plasma reagin (RPR) or treponemal test; treat with benzathine penicillin G.

A patient with chronic dysuria and a tender, nodular prostate on DRE; PSA is 4 ng/mL. How do you differentiate prostatitis from cancer? — Obtain urine culture and repeat PSA after infection treatment; consider transrectal biopsy if PSA remains elevated or nodule persists.

In a malaria‑endemic area, a man presents with scrotal swelling and fever; smear is negative for malaria. What infections should be considered and what empiric therapy is appropriate? — Consider bacterial epididymo‑orchitis (Chlamydia, gonorrhoea) and TB; start doxycycline plus ceftriaxone, add metronidazole if anaerobes suspected.

A 60‑year‑old man has lower urinary tract symptoms, a hard prostate on DRE, and PSA 12 ng/mL. What staging investigations are required? — Transrectal ultrasound, MRI of pelvis, and bone scan to assess local extension and metastasis.

Why is a scrotal ultrasound not sufficient to rule out testicular torsion in a low‑resource setting? — Ultrasound may be unavailable or operator‑dependent; clinical signs (high‑riding testis, absent cremasteric reflex) dictate urgent surgery.

What are the contraindications to using fluoroquinolones for prostatitis in a patient with sickle cell disease? — Fluoroquinolones can precipitate tendon rupture and have limited efficacy in intracellular organisms; consider trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole if susceptibility allows.

A patient with a longstanding hydrocele develops a firm nodule within the sac. What is the most likely diagnosis and next step? — Suspicion for testicular tumour; obtain scrotal ultrasound and refer for orchiectomy.
ai.title: Male Reproductive Pathology
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: An overview of common diseases of the penis, testes and prostate in low‑resource settings, focusing on clinical reasoning, diagnosis, staging and management without relying on advanced tests.

b: Penile lesions: ulcer, plaque, infection, tumour
Testicular masses: hydrocele, torsion, infection, tumour
Prostatic disease: prostatitis, benign enlargement, carcinoma
sections.p: Male reproductive pathology includes disorders of the penis, testes and prostate that cause pain, swelling, dysfunction or malignancy. Diagnosis rests on history, focused exam and basic investigations.

b: Testicular cancer: TNM (T1‑T4, N0‑N1, M0‑M1)
Prostate cancer: Gleason score + PSA level
Acute epididymo‑orchitis: <24 h vs >24 h
sections.p: Severity is graded by symptom burden, organ involvement and, for cancer, TNM stage; for prostatitis, acute vs chronic; for torsion, time since onset.

b: Penile ulcer: chancroid, syphilis, herpes, trauma
Testicular pain/swelling: bacterial epididymo‑orchitis (often sexually transmitted), malaria‑related orchitis, TB, trauma
Prostatic infection: sexually transmitted pathogens, urinary reflux, TB prostatitis
Malignancy: testicular germ‑cell tumour, prostate adenocarcinoma (rare before 50 y), penile squamous cell carcinoma
sections.p: In East Africa, infectious and inflammatory causes dominate, followed by trauma and malignancy.

b: Penile ulcer: painless ulcer with indurated base (syphilis) or painful ragged ulcer (chancroid)
Testicular torsion: sudden severe unilateral pain, high‑riding testis, absent cremasteric reflex
Acute epididymo‑orchitis: gradual pain, fever, tender epididymis, scrotal swelling
Prostatitis: dysuria, perineal pain, low‑grade fever, tender prostate on DRE
sections.p: Patients usually present with pain, swelling, discharge or urinary symptoms; systemic signs may suggest infection or malignancy.
When ultrasound is unavailable, rely on clinical signs (high‑riding testis, absent cremasteric reflex) and urgent surgical exploration.

t.b: Is the mass solid or fluid? Solid suggests tumour or torsion; fluid suggests hydrocele or epididymo‑orchitis
Is there pyuria or specific pathogen? Guides antibiotic choice

t.a: Serology for syphilis, HIV, hepatitis B
t.b: Positive serology explains ulcer aetiology and informs infection control

t.a: Serum AFP, β‑hCG, LDH (if cancer suspected)
t.b: Elevated markers support germ‑cell tumour; normal values do not exclude it
Is the prostate enlarged, nodular or tender? Distinguishes BPH, prostatitis and carcinoma

t.a: Fine‑needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) of testicular mass (if surgery delayed)
t.b: Provides cytology to guide urgent orchiectomy

b: Testicular torsion >6 h → irreversible infarction
Septic epididymo‑orchitis → abscess, infertility
Penile carcinoma → local invasion, lymph node spread
Prostate abscess → sepsis, urinary obstruction
sections.p: Identify conditions that can rapidly threaten fertility or life.

b: Torsion: immediate surgical detorsion ± orchiopexy; delay >24 h may need orchiectomy
Bacterial epididymo‑orchitis: doxycycline (or azithromycin) for Chlamydia, ceftriaxone for gonorrhoea; add metronidazole if anaerobes suspected
Penile ulcer: benzathine penicillin G for syphilis; azithromycin for chancroid; analgesia and wound care
Prostate infection: fluoroquinolone (e.g., ciprofloxacin) unless resistance suspected; avoid tetracyclines in severe renal impairment
Testicular cancer: radical inguinal orchiectomy followed by surveillance or chemotherapy based on stage
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care and monitor for complications.

b: Post‑torsion: review at 1 week for wound healing, ultrasound if doubt persists
Epididymo‑orchitis: repeat urine culture after 7 days; counsel on condom use
Penile cancer: monitor surgical margins, counsel on smoking cessation
Prostate disease: PSA repeat in 6 months if elevated; advise fluid intake and bladder training
sections.p: Schedule review based on diagnosis; educate on safe sex, hygiene and early presentation.

Varicocele vs epididymo‑orchitis
Benign prostatic hyperplasia vs prostate cancer
